strengths: Solid theoretical decomposition of worst-group error into spurious and core components with multiclass/multidomain extensions
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 6 datasets with 30+ baselines and multiple experimental settings
Consistent improvements across benchmarks, particularly strong on ColorMNIST and text datasets
Clear presentation with detailed appendix, algorithm pseudocode, and reproducibility details
Good qualitative analysis including Grad-CAM visualizations and correlation studies demonstrating the method's effectiveness
Modular design enabling integration with different worst-group losses and environment inference frameworks
weaknesses: Significant theory-practice gap: theory assumes linear classifiers and Gaussian distributions while method applies to deep networks on real data; justification that theoretical structure remains valid is insufficient
Restrictive theoretical assumptions (constant Δ_core/Δ_spur, balanced priors, extreme spurious correlations) rarely hold in practice, limiting validity of theoretical motivation
Marginal and inconsistent empirical improvements: Waterbirds 91.2% vs DFR 91.0% (0.2%), CelebA 91.4% vs ElRep 91.4% (tied), many within error bars; lacks statistical significance testing
Simplistic conceptualization of spurious vs core directions based solely on domain/class dimensions ignores within-domain spurious correlations and domain-specific legitimate feature variations
Requires explicit group/domain labels at training time, limiting practical applicability; integration with EIIL is workaround not core contribution
Hyperparameter sensitivity (λ_core, λ_spur) without principled guidance for practitioners; Tables 6-11 show non-trivial performance variation across settings
Questionable baseline results raise fairness concerns (e.g., LfF achieving 53% on CelebA vs other methods >70%)
Limited ablation studies on design choices; Σ-norm vs Euclidean comparison on only one dataset insufficient to justify selection
Incremental novelty building on existing embedding regularization methods (DFR, ElRep) without major conceptual innovation
Missing analysis of scalability, continuous domain attributes, high-dimensional spurious correlations, and multiple independent spurious factors

strengths: Clear and insightful theoretical decomposition of worst-group error into spurious and core components (Theorem 1), providing principled motivation for the regularization approach

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 6 datasets with consistent improvements in worst-group accuracy; includes challenging scenarios (missing groups, noisy environment labels) demonstrating robustness
Practical and modular design that integrates with existing frameworks (EIIL) without requiring additional group annotations; shows effectiveness even with imperfect environment information

Strong qualitative analysis with t-SNE and Grad-CAM visualizations that provide convincing evidence the method learns domain-invariant representations aligned with labels rather than spurious attributes
Thorough experimental protocol with 18+ baselines across multiple robustness categories and extensive ablations (Tables 6, 18) validating design choices
Well-written paper with clear presentation, detailed appendices supporting reproducibility, and honest discussion of theoretical limitations
weaknesses: Significant theory-practice gap: Theorem 1 assumes Gaussian embeddings, extreme spurious correlations (P(y,d)≈0), linear classifiers, and binary/2-domain settings, but is applied to deep networks with multi-class/multi-domain problems; the claim that Gaussian assumptions are 'empirically well-grounded' provides insufficient justification

Method novelty is incremental: GroupDRO already addresses worst-group robustness; SCER primarily adds straightforward embedding regularization (products of alignment and magnitude terms). The specific loss formulation design choices lack deep justification beyond the limited theory

Empirical improvements are often marginal: CelebA (91.4% vs 91.0%), MetaShift (86.7% vs 85.6%) improvements fall within or near standard deviations; practical significance unclear. Performance degrades substantially on ColorMNIST at ρ=99% (56.0%), limiting scalability

Methodological limitations inadequately addressed: (1) Group-wise mean decomposition assumes means capture essential variation—no validation for heterogeneous groups; (2) Method assumes spurious correlations specifically between domain and label, cannot handle other corruption types; (3) Σ-covariance stability from batches during training not analyzed; no ablation on this practical concern

Reproducibility concerns: Code URL is blank despite reproducibility claims. Hyperparameter selection process incomplete (unclear if per-dataset tuning used). Environment inference experiments limited to ColorMNIST with only one noisy setting (Table 14)

Experimental design issues: Group annotations used for model selection across all methods (Table 10), potentially favoring methods designed for group information. ElRep comparison shows variable results suggesting potential dataset-dependence of SCER's advantages

Theoretical robustness fragile: Remark about ±sign in Theorem 1 reveals outcome depends on initialization and training dynamics. Multi-class/multi-domain extensions are empirically validated but not theoretically justified

Missing key analyses: No ablation on why multiply (rather than other combinations) alignment by magnitude; no analysis of convergence properties; limited discussion of failure modes or settings where the spurious-core decomposition breaks down

strengths: Clear theoretical motivation with Theorem 1 decomposing worst-group error into spurious and core components, providing formal justification for the embedding regularization approach

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 6 datasets (vision and language) with multiple spurious correlation levels and extreme scenarios (missing groups, noisy environment inference, ρ up to 99%)
Consistent empirical improvements, particularly strong on extreme cases (59.6% worst-group accuracy vs 44.1% for next best on ColorMNIST with one group omitted)
Extensive qualitative analysis including t-SNE embeddings, Grad-CAM visualizations, and correlation analysis that effectively validate the theoretical insights
Practical applicability demonstrated through integration with environment inference methods (EIIL) without requiring explicit bias labels
Thorough reproducibility standards with detailed experimental setup, hyperparameter search spaces, multiple random seeds, and promised code release
Rigorous baseline comparisons against 17+ methods including recent strong baselines (LISA, PDE, ElRep)
weaknesses: Restrictive theoretical assumptions including Gaussian mixture model with shared covariance, constant spurious/core directions across domains/labels, and extreme spurious correlations (P(y,d)≈0 for some pairs) that limit the scope of theoretical guarantees
Gap between theory and practice: Theorem 1 assumes optimal ERM solution β* ∝ Σ⁻¹Δ̃ but algorithms use current neural network weights during training; implications not deeply analyzed

Modest empirical improvements over strong recent baselines on some datasets (e.g., 91.2% vs 90.3% PDE on Waterbirds, 74.0% vs 73.7% LISA on CivilComments), with improvements sometimes within error margins

Hyperparameter selection in practice requires group labels at validation time for model selection, limiting applicability to scenarios without group annotations; EIIL experiments partially address but are limited
Limited theoretical analysis of multi-class case; Theorem 1 only covers binary classification
Incomplete justification for Σ-norm choice over alternatives; Table 7 shows only one dataset comparison, lacking systematic analysis of when this normalization is optimal
Insufficient discussion of failure modes and scalability: why does performance degrade significantly at ρ=99%? How does method scale to very high-dimensional embeddings?
Missing ablation studies on individual components; Table 6/18 sensitivity analysis only on two datasets
No formal statistical significance testing provided despite reporting standard deviations
